# Customizing opencode

opencode validates its own config strictly and refuses to start when a field
is wrong. The shapes below cover the common surface area, but they are a
**summary, not the source of truth**.

## Full schema reference

The authoritative list of every config option — with field types, enums,
defaults, and descriptions — lives in the published JSON Schema:

**<https://opencode.ai/config.json>**

If a field is not documented in this skill, or you need to confirm an exact
shape before writing config, **fetch that URL and read the schema directly**
rather than guessing. opencode hard-fails on invalid config, so the cost of a
wrong shape is a broken startup.

Independently, every `opencode.json` should declare
`"$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json"` so the user's editor catches
mistakes as they type.

## Applying changes

Config is loaded once when opencode starts and is not hot-reloaded. After
saving changes to `opencode.json`, an agent file, a skill, a plugin, or any
other config-time file, **tell the user to quit and restart opencode** for
the changes to take effect. The running session will keep using the
already-loaded config until then.

## Where files live

| Scope                         | Path                                                                                                                      |
| ----------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Project config                | `./opencode.json`, `./opencode.jsonc`, or `.opencode/opencode.json` (opencode walks up from the cwd to the worktree root) |
| Global config                 | `~/.config/opencode/opencode.json` (NOT `~/.opencode/`)                                                                   |
| Project agents                | `.opencode/agent/<name>.md` or `.opencode/agents/<name>.md`                                                               |
| Global agents                 | `~/.config/opencode/agent(s)/<name>.md`                                                                                   |
| Project commands              | `.opencode/command/<name>.md` or `.opencode/commands/<name>.md`                                                           |
| Global commands               | `~/.config/opencode/command(s)/<name>.md`                                                                                 |
| Project skills                | `.opencode/skill(s)/<name>/SKILL.md`                                                                                      |
| Global skills                 | `~/.config/opencode/skill(s)/<name>/SKILL.md`                                                                             |
| External skills (auto-loaded) | `~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`, `~/.agents/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`                                                    |

Configs from each scope are deep-merged. Project overrides global. Unknown
top-level keys in `opencode.json` are rejected with `ConfigInvalidError`.

## opencode.json

Every field is optional.

```json
{
  "$schema": "https://opencode.ai/config.json",
  "username": "string",
  "model": "provider/model-id",
  "small_model": "provider/model-id",
  "default_agent": "agent-name",
  "shell": "/bin/zsh",
  "logLevel": "DEBUG" | "INFO" | "WARN" | "ERROR",
  "share": "manual" | "auto" | "disabled",
  "autoupdate": true | false | "notify",
  "snapshot": true,
  "instructions": ["AGENTS.md", "docs/style.md"],

  "skills": {
    "paths": [".opencode/skills", "/abs/path/to/skills"],
    "urls": ["https://example.com/.well-known/skills/"]
  },

  "references": {
    "docs": {
      "path": "../docs",
      "description": "Use for product behavior and documentation conventions"
    },
    "sdk": {
      "repository": "owner/sdk",
      "branch": "main",
      "description": "Use for SDK implementation details",
      "hidden": true
    }
  },

  "agent": {
    "my-agent": {
      "model": "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6",
      "mode": "subagent",
      "description": "...",
      "permission": { "edit": "deny" }
    }
  },

  "command": {
    "deploy": { "description": "...", "template": "..." }
  },

  "provider": {
    "anthropic": { "options": { "apiKey": "..." } }
  },
  "disabled_providers": ["openai"],
  "enabled_providers": ["anthropic"],

  "mcp": {
    "playwright": {
      "type": "local",
      "command": ["npx", "-y", "@playwright/mcp"],
      "enabled": true,
      "env": {}
    },
    "remote-thing": {
      "type": "remote",
      "url": "https://...",
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer ..." }
    }
  },

  "plugin": [
    "opencode-gemini-auth",
    "opencode-foo@1.2.3",
    "./local-plugin.ts",
    ["opencode-bar", { "option": "value" }]
  ],

  "permission": {
    "edit": "deny",
    "bash": { "git *": "allow", "*": "ask" }
  },

  "formatter": false,
  "lsp": false,

  "experimental": {
    "primary_tools": ["edit"],
    "mcp_timeout": 30000
  },

  "tool_output": { "max_lines": 200, "max_bytes": 8192 },

  "compaction": { "auto": true, "tail_turns": 15 }
}
```

Shape notes worth being explicit about:

- `model` always carries a provider prefix: `"anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6"`.
- `skills` is an object with `paths` and/or `urls`, not an array.
- `references` is an object keyed by alias. Each value is a local path, Git repository, or string shorthand.
- `agent` is an object keyed by agent name, not an array.
- `command` is an object keyed by command name, not an array.
- `plugin` is an array of strings or `[name, options]` tuples, not an object.
- `mcp[name].command` is an array of strings, never a single string. `type` is required.
- `permission` is either a string action or an object keyed by tool name.

## Skills

opencode's skill loader scans for `**/SKILL.md` inside skill directories. The
file is named `SKILL.md` exactly, and lives in its own folder named after the
skill:

```
.opencode/skills/my-skill/SKILL.md
```

Frontmatter:

```markdown
---
name: my-skill
description: One sentence covering what this skill does AND when to trigger it. Front-load the literal keywords or filenames the user is likely to say.
---

# My Skill

(skill body in markdown: instructions, examples, references)
```

- `name` is required, lowercase hyphen-separated, up to 64 chars, and matches the folder name.
- `description` is effectively required: skills without one are filtered out and never surfaced to the model. Cover both _what_ the skill does and _when_ to use it. Write in third person ("Use when...", not "I help with..."). Front-load concrete trigger keywords and filenames; gate with "Use ONLY when..." if the skill should stay quiet on adjacent topics.
- Optional: `license`, `compatibility`, `metadata` (string-string map).

Register skills from non-default locations via `skills.paths` (scanned
recursively for `**/SKILL.md`) and `skills.urls` (each URL serves a list of
skills).

## References

References make local directories and Git repositories outside the active
project available as supporting context. Configure them under `references`,
keyed by the alias used in `@` autocomplete:

```json
{
  "references": {
    "docs": {
      "path": "../product-docs",
      "description": "Use for product behavior and terminology"
    },
    "effect": {
      "repository": "Effect-TS/effect",
      "branch": "main",
      "description": "Use for Effect implementation details"
    }
  }
}
```

Local `path` values may be relative to the declaring config, absolute, or use
`~/`. Git `repository` values accept Git URLs, host/path references, and GitHub
`owner/repo` shorthand; `branch` is optional. Both forms support optional
`description` and `hidden` fields.

- Only references with a `description` are advertised to agents in system context.
- `hidden: true` removes a reference from TUI `@` autocomplete only. It remains available to agents and by direct path.
- Reference directories are automatically allowed through the external-directory boundary; normal read/edit/tool permissions still apply.
- String shorthand is supported: use `"docs": "../docs"` for local paths or `"effect": "Effect-TS/effect"` for Git repositories.

## Agents

Two ways to define an agent. Use the file form for anything non-trivial.

### Inline (in `opencode.json`)

```json
{
  "agent": {
    "my-reviewer": {
      "description": "Reviews PRs for style violations.",
      "mode": "subagent",
      "model": "anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6",
      "permission": { "edit": "deny", "bash": "ask" },
      "prompt": "You are a strict PR reviewer..."
    }
  }
}
```

### File

```
.opencode/agent/my-reviewer.md      OR     .opencode/agents/my-reviewer.md
```

```markdown
---
description: Reviews PRs for style violations.
mode: subagent
model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6
permission:
  edit: deny
  bash: ask
---

You are a strict PR reviewer. Focus on...
```

The file body becomes the agent's `prompt`. Do not also put `prompt:` in the
frontmatter.

`mode` is one of `"primary"`, `"subagent"`, `"all"`.

Allowed top-level frontmatter fields: `name, model, variant, description, mode,
hidden, color, steps, options, permission, disable, temperature, top_p`. Any
unknown field is silently routed into `options`.

To disable a built-in agent: `agent: { build: { disable: true } }`, or in a
file, `disable: true` in frontmatter.

`default_agent` must point to a non-hidden, primary-mode agent.

### Built-in agents

opencode ships with `build`, `plan`, `general`, `explore`. Hidden internal agents:
`compaction`, `title`, `summary`. To override a built-in's fields, define the
same key in `agent: { <name>: { ... } }`.

## Commands

opencode's command loader scans for `**/*.md` inside command directories. The
file is named after the command, and lives directly inside the `command` folder:

```
.opencode/command/deploy.md
```

Frontmatter:

```markdown
---
description: One sentence describing what the command does.
agent: build
model: anthropic/claude-sonnet-4-6
---

(command body in markdown: the prompt opencode runs, with  for the user's input)
```

- `template` is the command body — everything below the frontmatter — and is required: it is the prompt opencode runs when the command is invoked. Do not also put a `template:` key in the frontmatter.
- `` is replaced with everything the user typed after the command; ``, ``, … pull individual positional arguments.
- Optional: `description`, `agent`, `model`, `variant`, `subtask`.

## Plugins

`plugin:` is an array. Each entry is one of:

```json
"plugin": [
  "opencode-gemini-auth",            // npm spec, latest
  "opencode-foo@1.2.3",              // npm spec, pinned
  "./local-plugin.ts",               // file path, relative to the declaring config
  "file:///abs/path/plugin.js",      // file URL
  ["opencode-bar", { "key": "val" }] // tuple form with options
]
```

Auto-discovered plugins (no config entry needed): any `*.ts` or `*.js` file in
`.opencode/plugin/` or `.opencode/plugins/`.

A plugin module exports `default` (or any named export) of type
`Plugin = (input: PluginInput, options?) => Promise<Hooks>`. The export is a
function, not a plain object literal, and the function returns an object
(return `{}` if there is nothing to register).

```ts
import type { Plugin } from "@opencode-ai/plugin"

export default (async ({ client, project, directory, $ }) => {
  return {
    config: (cfg) => {
      // cfg is the live merged config; mutate fields here.
    },
    "tool.execute.before": async (input, output) => {
      // mutate output.args before the tool runs
    },
  }
}) satisfies Plugin
```

Hook surface (mutate `output` in place; return `void`):

- `event(input)`: every bus event
- `config(cfg)`: once on init with the merged config
- `chat.message`, `chat.params`, `chat.headers`
- `tool.execute.before`, `tool.execute.after`
- `tool.definition`
- `command.execute.before`
- `shell.env`
- `permission.ask`
- `experimental.chat.messages.transform`, `experimental.chat.system.transform`,
  `experimental.session.compacting`, `experimental.compaction.autocontinue`,
  `experimental.text.complete`

Special object-shaped (not callbacks): `tool: { my_tool: { ... } }`,
`auth: { ... }`, `provider: { ... }`.

## MCP servers

`mcp:` is an object keyed by server name. Each server is discriminated by
`type`:

```json
{
  "mcp": {
    "playwright": {
      "type": "local",
      "command": ["npx", "-y", "@playwright/mcp"],
      "enabled": true,
      "env": { "BROWSER": "chromium" }
    },
    "github": {
      "type": "remote",
      "url": "https://...",
      "enabled": true,
      "headers": { "Authorization": "Bearer {env:GITHUB_TOKEN}" }
    },
    "old-server": { "enabled": false }
  }
}
```

`command` is an array of strings. `type` is required. Use `enabled: false` to
disable a server inherited from a parent config. String values such as header
tokens support `{env:VAR}` interpolation (and `{file:path}`); the shell-style
`${VAR}` is not substituted.

## Permissions

```json
"permission": {
  "edit": "deny",
  "bash": { "git *": "allow", "rm *": "deny", "*": "ask" },
  "external_directory": { "~/secrets/**": "deny", "*": "allow" }
}
```

Actions: `"allow"`, `"ask"`, `"deny"`.

Per-tool value forms: `"allow"` shorthand (treated as `{"*": "allow"}`), or an
object `{ pattern: action }`. Within an object, **insertion order matters**.
opencode evaluates the LAST matching rule, so put broad rules first and narrow
rules last.

`permission: "allow"` (a string at the top level) is shorthand for "allow
everything" and is rarely what the user wants.

Known permission keys: `read, edit, glob, grep, list, bash, task,
external_directory, todowrite, question, webfetch, websearch, lsp, doom_loop,
skill`. Some of these (`todowrite,
question, webfetch, websearch, doom_loop`) only accept a flat
action, not a per-pattern object.

`external_directory` patterns are filesystem paths (use `~/`, absolute paths,
or globs like `~/projects/**`).

Per-agent `permission:` overrides top-level `permission:`. Plan Mode lives on
the `plan` agent's permission ruleset (`edit: deny *`).

## Escape hatches

When a user's config is broken and opencode won't start, these env vars help:

- `OPENCODE_DISABLE_PROJECT_CONFIG=1`: skip the project's local `opencode.json`
  and start from globals only. Run from the project directory, opencode loads,
  the user edits the broken file, then they restart without the flag.
- `OPENCODE_CONFIG=/path/to/file.json`: load an additional explicit config.
- `OPENCODE_CONFIG_CONTENT='{"$schema":"https://opencode.ai/config.json"}'`:
  inject inline JSON as a final local-scope merge.
- `OPENCODE_DISABLE_DEFAULT_PLUGINS=1`: skip default plugins.
- `OPENCODE_PURE=1`: skip external plugins entirely.
- `OPENCODE_DISABLE_EXTERNAL_SKILLS=1`,
  `OPENCODE_DISABLE_CLAUDE_CODE_SKILLS=1`: skip the external skill scans under
  `~/.claude/` and `~/.agents/`.

## When proposing edits

- Validate against the schema before writing. If you are unsure of a field's
  exact shape, or the field is not covered in this skill, fetch
  `https://opencode.ai/config.json` and read the schema rather than guessing.
- Preserve `$schema` and any existing fields the user did not ask to change.
- For agent, command, skill, and plugin definitions, prefer creating new files
  in the correct location over inlining everything in `opencode.json`.
- If the user's existing config is malformed, point them at the env-var escape
  hatches above so they can edit from inside opencode without breaking their
  session.
- After saving any config change, remind the user to quit and restart opencode
  — running sessions keep using the already-loaded config.

# 9. Load timing versus duplicate package/context

## Ordinary remote loading timing

Every identified `useAuth()` occurs inside a component or hook at render time. None is evaluated at module top level.

Therefore:

1. remote JavaScript can load before the provider;
2. the component can later be rendered below the provider;
3. `useContext` then reads the provider’s current value.

The import does not permanently capture the default context value.

In the current host, children are underneath dynamically loaded provider components, so they are not rendered first and wrapped later:

- `D:\work\qcash-ui\pages\_app.tsx:169-192`
- `D:\work\qcash-ui\components\providers\BRIProviders.tsx:46-50`

## Auth hydration timing

This can matter transiently.

The provider synchronously initializes only the token from local storage:

- `D:\work\qcash-global-component\node_modules\@ordentco\addons-auth-provider\dist\src\auth.js:234-239`

Username, user type, company IDs and authorities initially remain defaults:

- `...dist\src\auth.js:241-252`

`guard()` later hydrates them and sets readiness:

- cached hydration: `...dist\src\auth.js:275-303`
- validation starts with readiness false: `...dist\src\auth.js:320-330`
- completed authorities become ready: `...dist\src\auth.js:446-449`

The remote project itself does not call `guard()` from `_app`. The current host calls it asynchronously through `AuthBridgeSync`:

- `D:\work\qcash-ui\components\providers\AuthBridgeSync.ts:271-287`

None of the remote’s exposed auth consumers checks `isAuthoritiesReady`. Thus they can briefly render Guest/disabled/hidden states before hydration. With the correct context instance they should rerender afterward.

## Duplicate auth-package instance

If the host has package instance A and the remote consumes package instance B:

```text
Host AuthProvider_A
  └─ Remote component
       └─ useAuth_B() → AuthContext_B default
```

React ancestry alone cannot bridge `AuthContext_A` to `AuthContext_B`; the context object identity is different. This produces persistent Guest/null/false values and default callbacks even after host auth is ready.

## Duplicate React instance

If the host renderer uses React A while the remote hook uses React B, the common outcome is an invalid-hook-call/null-dispatcher error rather than merely Guest defaults.

Thus:

- **Guest/null/false without an invalid-hook error:** suspect duplicate auth context or no provider.
- **Invalid hook call:** suspect duplicate React.
- **Defaults that later correct themselves:** suspect normal auth hydration timing.
- **Behavior changing according to which remote initializes first:** suspect share-version/scope negotiation.

`ConfirmModal` reads user type and global store:

- `D:\work\qcash-global-component\components\confirm-modal\index.tsx:63-75`

- `confirm-modal\index.tsx:76,84-91`

## 10.7 `useGlobalStore`-only exposure renders the wrong OTP branch

`./modal-single-action` reads default `bricamsUser`:

- `D:\work\qcash-global-component\components\advanced-table\modal-single-action.tsx:18,86`

With default `{}`, `bricamsUser?.idToken` is `undefined`. Since `undefined !== ""`, the component can enter the “token exists” branch:

- warning branch: `modal-single-action.tsx:458-464`
- OTP-input branch: `modal-single-action.tsx:466-490`

This is a concrete reason that both Auth and GlobalStore contexts must match.

---

# Recommended interpretation and corrective actions

1. **Do not rely on the remote `_app`; it never wraps remote consumers.**
2. Ensure the host provides both `AuthProvider` and `GlobalStoreProvider` from the same shared package factory.
3. Mark `@ordentco/addons-auth-provider` as `singleton: true` in the host as well as the remote.
4. Align host and remote auth versions instead of relying on `requiredVersion: false`.
5. Align React/ReactDOM versions and verify they resolve from one share scope.
6. Ensure runtime-loaded remotes are initialized with the same webpack/default share scope.
7. Gate authority-sensitive components on `isAuthoritiesReady` to prevent transient authorization UI.
8. Remove lock drift and use one package manager with a frozen lock.
9. Add a host-level integration test that renders an exposed auth-sensitive component under the real shared providers; current component tests largely mock `useAuth`, so they do not validate Module Federation context identity.

The strongest diagnostic distinction is: **persistent defaults indicate missing/duplicate context; transient defaults indicate hydration; invalid-hook errors indicate duplicate React.**

## Conclusion

The exact symptom is most consistent with navigation being performed by the federated header’s `next/router` instance rather than the host Pages Router instance:

1. `router.push()` updates `window.history`, so the URL changes.
2. The host Pages Router does not receive/complete the route transition.
3. Its current page component—Issuance LC—therefore remains mounted.

There is no active navigation blocker in the Issuance LC page itself. A previously committed header/footer fix explicitly recognizes this exact Issuance-LC-only problem and forces a document navigation when leaving it.

## Ranked root causes

### 1. Known header navigation/context defect; its hard-navigation fix is currently disabled

Confidence: very high.

The header/footer repository contains an Issuance-specific hard-navigation list:

- `D:\work\qcash-ui-header-footer\layouts\default\container\menu\components\MenuModalProvider.tsx:37-39`

```ts
const REGISTERED_HARD_NAV_PAGES = [
  "/v2/import-lc/issuance-lc",
];
```

The corresponding workaround is currently commented out in the working tree:

- `D:\work\qcash-ui-header-footer\layouts\default\container\menu\components\MenuModalProvider.tsx:93-101`

Consequently, navigation falls through to:

- `D:\work\qcash-ui-header-footer\layouts\default\container\menu\components\MenuModalProvider.tsx:108-117`

```ts
router.push(`/${_href}`);
```

The header gets that router from its own federated bundle:

- `D:\work\qcash-ui-header-footer\layouts\default\container\menu\components\MenuModalProvider.tsx:2`
- `D:\work\qcash-ui-header-footer\layouts\default\container\menu\components\MenuModalProvider.tsx:43`

This is precisely capable of producing “URL changes, old page remains” when its `next/router` resolves to a different router/module context than the host’s.

This was already fixed by:

- Commit `8161f7cc`: `fix: document navigation when leaving issuance LC`
- Commit `8a867362`: `fix[NQLA-60919] - adjust navigation issue next route missing context`

The committed fix was:

```ts
if (globalThis.window.location.pathname.startsWith("/v2/import-lc/issuance-lc")) {
  globalThis.window.location.href = href;
  return;
}
```

The current header/footer working tree has locally commented that fix out while adding navigation diagnostics. If that state reflects the failing deployment, this is the immediate cause. Otherwise, verify that the deployed/cached header `remoteEntry.js` actually contains `8161f7cc` or later.

- `beforePopState`

   - Do not let the header resolve and call its own federated `next/router`.
2. Align Next, `@module-federation/nextjs-mf`, and `@module-federation/runtime` versions across host, header, and Issuance.
3. Remove repeated page-level `init()` calls; initialize federation once in the host.
4. Align the auth-provider version and remove its dependency on `next/router`.

Investigate D:\work\addons-auth-provider thoroughly. This is read-only diagnosis; do not edit files. Trace the AuthContext creation, default values, AuthProvider implementation, real guard function, useAuth export, package build/output, and any conditions under which useAuth can return the default throwing `Function not implemented.` guard despite an AuthProvider apparently existing. Check package name/version and git history if useful. Return concise findings with exact file:line references and a concrete runtime call path. Thoroughness: very thorough.

## Verdict

`useAuth()` can return the throwing default only when React cannot find the **same `AuthContext` object** above the consumer. There is no token, cache, API, loading, or provider-state path that replaces the real guard with the default guard.

Therefore, if the stack resolves to `dist/src/auth.js:126` or source-maps to `src/auth.tsx:169`, the consumer is either:

1. Outside the matching provider’s React ancestry, or
2. Using a second evaluation/copy of the auth package: `Context_A !== Context_B`.

The second case is the strongest risk in the current Module Federation setup.

## Package trace

- Package is `@bri/addons-auth-provider` version `0.10.8-mfe`; runtime entry is `dist/src/index.js`:  
  `D:\work\addons-auth-provider\package.json:2-6`
- Root entry requires one CJS auth module and re-exports its provider and hook:  
  `D:\work\addons-auth-provider\dist\src\index.js:4-7`
- Defaults include guest/null/empty state and throwing implementations for guard, login/logout, permission methods and setters:  
  `D:\work\addons-auth-provider\src\auth.tsx:146-281`  
  `D:\work\addons-auth-provider\dist\src\auth.js:96-263`
- The default guard is asynchronous, so it returns a rejected promise containing the error:  
  `D:\work\addons-auth-provider\src\auth.tsx:168-170`  
  `D:\work\addons-auth-provider\dist\src\auth.js:118-129`
- That object is passed directly to `createContext`; the context itself is private:  
  `D:\work\addons-auth-provider\src\auth.tsx:287`  
  `D:\work\addons-auth-provider\dist\src\auth.js:267`
- `useAuth` is only `useContext(AuthContext)` and performs no missing-provider check:  
  `D:\work\addons-auth-provider\src\auth.tsx:1284`  
  `D:\work\addons-auth-provider\dist\src\auth.js:1195-1196`

### Real provider and guard

- `AuthProvider` initializes its state immediately; no effect is required before a real guard exists:  
  `D:\work\addons-auth-provider\src\auth.tsx:309-360`
- The real guard is created with `useCallback`:  
  `D:\work\addons-auth-provider\src\auth.tsx:362-613`  
  `D:\work\addons-auth-provider\dist\src\auth.js:318-524`

- Provider and hook come from different package copies or versions.

I’ll inspect the referenced session artifact and trace the base-path request through Next.js routing, middleware, and the dashboard page before changing anything.

The previous session isolated the production 500 to the standalone server bundle, not the page route: `/dashboard` worked locally while `/` initially mapped to a 404, then both returned 200 only after forcing missing ESM dependencies into output tracing. I’m checking whether that proven fix was ever applied to this worktree and whether the deployed endpoint still exhibits the same failure.

The fix was tested only in a temporary clone during the earlier session and never copied into this repository, so the deployed image still has the exact same 500. I’m applying the two tracing includes to `next.config.ts`; no page or host-route change is needed.

The production build passes and now emits both `/` and `/dashboard`. Before starting it, I’m confirming the standalone artifact contains the previously missing files and that the container copies Next static assets into the runtime image.

The standalone server now returns `200` for both `/dashboard-auto-collection-v2` and `/dashboard-auto-collection-v2/dashboard`, and each response references the correct page bundle. I’m doing the final config lint and diff check; deployment is the only remaining step outside this worktree.

Fixed `next.config.ts:8`: standalone output now includes missing `i18next` and `react-i18next` ESM files.

- `yarn build`: passed
- Both local standalone routes return `200`
- Deployed URL remains `500` until this change is rebuilt and deployed.
okay explain to me what did you change and why the error happen on the first place

**What Changed**
In `next.config.ts:8`, I added:

```ts
outputFileTracingIncludes: {
  "/*": [
    "node_modules/i18next/dist/esm/**/*",
    "node_modules/react-i18next/dist/es/**/*",
  ],
},
```

This tells Next.js to copy those ESM files into `.next/standalone` for every route.

**Why It Failed**
`src/pages/index.tsx` already existed and was correctly mapped to:

`/dashboard-auto-collection-v2`

The failure occurred during production runtime:

1. `yarn build` generated server code importing `i18next` and `react-i18next`.
2. Next.js standalone file tracing failed to include their ESM files.
3. The deployed server tried to load files such as:
   - `i18next/dist/esm/i18next.js`
   - `react-i18next/dist/es/index.js`
4. Node could not find them, so Next.js returned `500 Internal Server Error` before the browser could render `index.tsx`.

This was likely caused by the experimental Next.js/Rspack build not detecting these dynamically imported dependencies during standalone tracing.

After explicitly including them, both standalone routes return `200`:

- `/dashboard-auto-collection-v2`
- `/dashboard-auto-collection-v2/dashboard`

That confirms it: the modal is the **"Select LC to be Amended or Cancelled"** modal rendered by [`IndexContainer`](file:///D:/work/qcash-ui-amend-cancel-lc/new-containers/index.tsx#L19-L40) using QUI's [`QuiModal`](file:///D:/work/qcash-ui-design-system/packages/components/src/components/modal/modal.tsx#L1-L245) (`ModalBackdrop` + `ModalContainer` + `ModalDialog`). --- ### Root Cause: Why the Session Expired Modal is Blocked Even though the Session Expired modal is visually on top (`z-index: 99999` vs QUI Modal `z-index: 50`), you cannot interact with it because of how **QUI's Modal (built on React Aria Components)** manages modal focus and overlays: #### 1. React Aria Focus Trap (`FocusScope`) * When [`QuiModal`](file:///D:/work/qcash-ui-design-system/packages/components/src/components/modal/modal.tsx#L85-L98) (`ModalOverlayPrimitive`) opens, React Aria registers a **capture-phase listener on `document`** (`document.addEventListener('focusin', ..., true)`). * When a user attempts to click an input, button, or link inside the Session Expired modal (`#session-expired-portal-root`), the `focusin` event hits the document capture listener. * React Aria's focus manager checks if the clicked element belongs to the active `QuiModal` DOM subtree. Because `#session-expired-portal-root` is outside the QUI Modal, React Aria treats it as an invalid focus escape and **immediately pulls focus back into the `QuiModal` dialog**, effectively freezing the Session Expired inputs. #### 2. React Aria `ariaHideOutside` and Pointer Capture * React Aria sets `data-react-aria-hidden="true"` and blocks interactions on all outside DOM nodes. * While [`SessionExpiredNewLayout.tsx`](file:///D:/work/qcash-ui/components/ui/SessionExpiredNewLayout.tsx#L69-L85) uses a `MutationObserver` to remove native `inert` and `aria-hidden` attributes, that **only handles DOM attributes**—it does not stop React Aria's active JavaScript `focusin` / `pointerdown` capture listeners. --- ### How to Fix This The fix needs to be applied in **[`qcash-ui`](file:///D:/work/qcash-ui/components/ui/SessionExpiredNewLayout.tsx)** so the Session Expired modal is immune to focus trapping from any active modal (QUI / React Aria or Headless UI): #### In [`qcash-ui/components/ui/SessionExpiredNewLayout.tsx`](file:///D:/work/qcash-ui/components/ui/SessionExpiredNewLayout.tsx): Stop capture-phase events (`focusin`, `pointerdown`, `mousedown`, `keydown`) from propagating up to `document`: ```tsx
e.stopPropagation()} onPointerDownCapture={(e) => e.stopPropagation()} onMouseDownCapture={(e) => e.stopPropagation()} onKeyDownCapture={(e) => e.stopPropagation()} > {/* Modal Content */}
``` **Why this works:** Stopping event propagation during the **capture phase** prevents React Aria's document-level focus trap and outside-click listeners from ever seeing events originating inside the Session Expired modal.

I’ll first inspect the project workspace and relevant prior context, then confirm the few product choices that materially affect the offline architecture and quickest logging flow.

The target folder is empty, but the vault contains prior work on a similarly named mobile FitFlow app. I’m checking whether that history reflects decisions worth preserving or an unrelated prototype, so the new plan does not accidentally inherit cloud/auth complexity you explicitly do not want.

Yes, this is fully possible. “No database” should mean no server/cloud database: the APK can keep everything privately in an on-device SQLite file, with no account, API, internet permission, analytics, or publishing; I also recommend an optional manual backup/export because uninstalling the app or losing the phone otherwise loses all history.

The main design decision is meal tracking: automatic calorie lookup normally needs an online service or a very large bundled food catalog. For an offline personal app, the fastest reliable workflow is reusable foods/meals plus recent items and one-tap repeat, with calories/macros entered only when creating an item.

## Proposed Project

**FitFlow** will be an Android-first React Native app that runs entirely offline.

- No login or account
- No backend or cloud database
- No Supabase, Firebase, APIs, analytics, or advertisements
- No internet required after installation
- Installed directly as a local APK
- Data stored privately in an SQLite file on the phone
- Manual backup and restore through a versioned JSON file

SQLite is technically a database, but it is embedded inside the APK’s private storage. Nothing is transmitted anywhere. A structured local store is significantly safer and more reliable than maintaining several raw JSON files.

## Core Experience

The home screen will prioritize one-tap logging rather than displaying long forms.

**Today**
- Current weight and latest measurements
- Calories consumed today
- Latest fitness results
- Large quick actions: `Weight`, `Measurements`, `Meal`, `Workout`
- Recent entries with quick edit and delete

**Weight**
- Tap `Weight`
- Numeric keypad opens immediately
- Current date and time selected automatically
- Previous weight shown for reference
- Enter kilograms and save
- Weight history and trend chart

**Measurements**
- One compact screen with exactly:
  - Waist
  - Biceps
  - Calf
- Measurements use centimeters
- No left/right distinction
- Previous values shown beside each field
- Date defaults to today
- One save button

**Meals**
- Calories only, without mandatory macro tracking
- Create a saved item once, such as `Chicken rice, 650 kcal`
- Log saved or recent items with one tap
- Quick portion choices such as `0.5x`, `1x`, `1.5x`, and `2x`
- Save combinations as reusable meal templates
- Show today’s calorie total and optional daily target
- Allow a quick custom calorie entry without creating a favorite

**Fitness**
- Strength entry: exercise, kilograms, and repetitions
- Push-up entry: repetitions
- Plank entry: duration
- Saved exercises and recent-performance shortcuts
- Quick repeat of the previous result
- Personal-best indicators
- Performance history charts per exercise

## Navigation

Four primary tabs keep the structure manageable:

1. **Today**: overview and quick logging
2. **Meals**: daily calorie log, favorites, and templates
3. **Fitness**: strength, push-ups, plank, and history
4. **Progress**: weight, measurements, and charts

Settings and backup will be accessible from the Today screen header.

## Local Data Model

The application will maintain these local records:

- `weight_entries`
- `body_measurements`
- `saved_meals`
- `meal_templates`
- `meal_log_entries`
- `exercises`
- `fitness_entries`
- `settings`

Each record will include a local ID and timestamp. SQLite schema migrations will allow future versions of the APK to update without deleting existing history.

## Backup Safety

The Settings screen will provide:

- `Export backup`
- `Import backup`
- `Delete all data`

The exported JSON will contain a schema version and all app data. Restore will validate the file before replacing existing data and require confirmation.

Without a backup, Android may erase the private data when the app is uninstalled. The app will periodically remind you to export one.

## Technical Plan

- React Native with Expo and TypeScript
- Expo Router for navigation
- `expo-sqlite` for on-device persistence
- `expo-file-system`, document picker, and sharing for backup
- Lightweight chart components for progress
- Android portrait layout
- Local release APK using `npx expo run:android --variant release`
- Production Android configuration that does not request internet access
- No authentication or network-state code

The archived `mobile-fitflow` prototype used authentication, Supabase, API clients, and React Query. This project should be created fresh in the empty `D:\code\fitflow` folder rather than inheriting that cloud architecture.

## Implementation Order

1. Scaffold the Expo TypeScript application and Android configuration.
2. Add the visual theme, navigation, and reusable controls.
3. Implement SQLite initialization, migrations, and repositories.
4. Build the Today dashboard and quick-entry sheets.
5. Implement weight and the three body measurements.
6. Implement calorie-only favorites, templates, recent meals, and daily totals.
7. Implement strength, push-up, and plank performance tracking.
8. Add histories, progress charts, personal bests, and editing.
9. Add validated backup export/import and data deletion.
10. Test offline behavior, persistence after restart, restore handling, and APK installation.
11. Produce a locally installable Android APK.

**Photo Flow**

- Store only photo metadata in SQLite:

  - Capture timestamp
  - Import source

- Imported photos remain available even if the original gallery photo is deleted.
- Camera photos remain private to FitFlow unless explicitly saved elsewhere.

fitflow-backup/
├── manifest.json
├── data.json
└── photos/

title: Faster vault scans and useful LLM features

messages.content:
i feel that there are some of the improvement we can make for this repo
1. i want to improve the scanning velocity of the vault scan command, it took very long time for now
2. we can add more useful feature for this llm, you can recommend me something for it
I’ll trace the scan pipeline to find where it repeats expensive work, then recommend features that support your earlier goal of having assistants consult the vault first.

I found a likely major bottleneck: each imported conversation triggers a read, parse, and rewrite of the entire `dataset.jsonl`. Scans also reprocess unchanged sessions, and OpenCode runs a separate database query for every message’s parts.

There’s also avoidable output churn: the Antigravity extractor assigns the current time on every scan, so unchanged conversations can still produce file changes. These findings come from code inspection; timing measurements will establish which costs dominate.

**I recommend two priorities: make scans incremental, then improve the quality of context returned to assistants.** Your feedback—that the delay happens before results appear, and better vault context matters most—fits what I found in the code.

## 1. Why `vault scan` is slow

These are confirmed implementation issues; their relative timing still needs measurement.

| Finding | Where | Impact |
|---|---|---|
| **The entire dataset is read, parsed, and rewritten for every conversation.** | `pkg/exporter/jsonl.go:55` | Likely the biggest bottleneck. Importing 500 sessions means processing the master dataset 500 times. |
| **Unchanged sessions are extracted, sanitized, audited, and exported again.** | `pkg/vault/vault.go:358` | Repeat scans do almost as much work as the first scan. |
| **OpenCode queries parts separately for every message.** | `pkg/extractor/opencode.go:124` | Large histories generate thousands of database queries. |
| **Assistant scans and session processing run sequentially.** | `pkg/vault/vault.go:358` | Independent work cannot overlap. |
| **Results appear only after all imports finish.** | `cmd/vault/main.go:121` | There is no indication of which source or stage is taking time. |

I also confirmed output churn: Antigravity assigns `time.Now()` to each extracted conversation. One existing Markdown diff contains **only a changed date**, despite identical content. Its language list also comes from unordered map iteration, which can destabilize content-derived IDs.

### Proposed scan improvements

**A. Batch dataset updates — first and highest priority**

- Collect imports into a scan-wide batch.
- Merge them with `dataset.jsonl` in one pass.
- Write the dataset once, using a temporary file and safe replacement.
- Avoid rewriting identical Markdown and ShareGPT exports.
- Preserve existing records and content-derived IDs.

This changes dataset work from “once per conversation” to “once per scan.”

**B. Add incremental scanning**

Keep a local, Git-ignored scan-state cache containing source fingerprints, processing versions, and corresponding export IDs.

- For file-based sessions, compare source size/modification time and use content hashes when needed.
- For OpenCode, track session changes using verified database revision fields, including message/part changes.
- Reprocess when sanitizer settings, custom redaction words, or extractor versions change.
- Retry failed or actively changing sources; record completion only after successful persistence.
- Recover missing outputs and provide a proposed `--full` option to force reprocessing.

An unchanged repeat scan should perform discovery and lightweight checks rather than extract and sanitize every conversation again.

**C. Optimize extraction and add progress**

- Batch OpenCode message/part queries.
- Introduce a bounded worker pool for extraction and sanitization, with one coordinated dataset writer.
- Stabilize timestamps and language ordering.
- Show live progress and phase durations, with separate counts for **new, changed, unchanged, trivial, and failed** sessions.

Since your delay is before the summary, I would address these first and measure the full audit separately.

## 2. Better context for your assistants

The current retrieval is very limited:

- `Search()` looks for the **entire query as one substring**.
- Results follow file traversal order rather than relevance.
- Context takes the first three matches and approximately five lines around each match.

Consequently, a query can miss a useful conversation because its wording differs—or retrieve the original question without the later solution.

### Recommended feature: ranked, project-aware context

**Local search index**
- Build a rebuildable index from sanitized exports.
- Update changed entries during scans and reconcile files added through Git pulls.
- Rank individual conversation passages using keyword relevance, phrase matches, and title matches.
- Support filters for project, assistant, and date.
- Prefer distinct, useful passages over repeated copies of the same discussion.

**Answer-focused context**
- Retrieve relevant user/assistant exchanges, including surrounding explanation and code.
- Include source file and turn references.
- Support a configurable context-size budget and result limit.
- Label archived content as historical reference.
- Apply the same retrieval engine to the CLI and dashboard.

**Project awareness**
- Capture project associations where source metadata supports them.
- Allow explicit project aliases for older sessions.
- Keep local filesystem mappings in the local cache.

Proposed usage after implementation:

```powershell
vault search "session expiration" --project qcash-ui --limit 10
vault context "why does the session expire early?" --project qcash-ui --max-chars 12000
```

I would start with ranked local text search. Semantic search can follow once we have examples to measure retrieval quality against.

## 3. Useful follow-up features

| Feature | Benefit | Priority |
|---|---|---|
| **Project memory cards** | Curated decisions, known fixes, and preferences with links to supporting sessions | Next |
| **MCP retrieval tools** | Let compatible assistants search and fetch vault context directly | After retrieval improvements |
| **Background incremental scans** | Keep context fresh automatically | After incremental scanning is reliable |

## Implementation order and verification

1. **Measure and fix batch storage**, including deterministic exports.
2. **Add incremental scans, optimized extraction, and progress.**
3. **Implement ranked context retrieval and dashboard integration.**

Verification should cover cold scans, unchanged repeats, one changed session, redaction-rule changes, interrupted writes, and missing exports. Retrieval tests should check that representative queries find the relevant explanation or fix with accurate citations.

**Success criteria:** unchanged repeat scans do not rewrite exports, the dataset is rewritten at most once per scan, and context results are relevance-ranked and source-linked.

No files have been changed during this planning review.

Yes—this fits the plan well. The current filename generator explicitly uses the first user message, even when the session has a better title. I’d replace that with a conversation-level title, while retaining the short ID suffix to prevent filename collisions.

Two choices affect the design: how titles are generated, and whether existing exports should be renamed too.

Yes—**we’ll add conversation-aware filenames for future imports, using offline rules.** Existing filenames will stay as they are.

### How the new naming will work

Instead of taking the opening words, the vault will:

1. **Evaluate the session’s existing title.** Use it if it is descriptive and supported by the conversation; reject generic titles such as “New session” or “Hello.”
2. **Analyze substantive messages throughout the conversation.** Look for recurring project names, components, errors, and actions across user requests and assistant explanations.
3. **Ignore naming noise.** Exclude greetings, pasted environment instructions, raw URLs, token-like strings, and repetitive tool output.
4. **Build a short topic-and-action name**, using sanitized text only.

Illustrative examples:

| Opening message | Main conversation topic | Better filename |
|---|---|---|
| “hello, can you check this…” | Debugging session expiration | `opencode_debug-session-expiration-<id>.md` |
| A long internal URL | Fixing a beneficiary edit modal | `antigravity_fix-beneficiary-edit-modal-<id>.md` |
| Pasted build output | Resolving TypeScript import errors | `codex_resolve-typescript-import-errors-<id>.md` |

These are examples of the intended naming style. Offline rules will produce descriptive topic labels, rather than always achieving the fluency of an AI-generated title.

### Keep names stable

- **Retain the short ID suffix** to prevent collisions.
- **Keep filename generation separate from content identity.** A naming-rule change must not create a new conversation ID.
- **Choose the filename when a conversation is first exported**, then retain that choice on repeat imports.
- Apply the same basename to its Markdown and ShareGPT files.
- Recognize existing exports by their IDs so rebuilding the local cache does not accidentally rename them.

For a session covering several unrelated tasks, favor its dominant topic or a concise broader label rather than an overly specific guess. Names also won’t claim an issue is “fixed” solely because a fix was requested.

### Fit with the performance work

Title selection will happen **after sanitization, only for newly exported conversations**, using bounded text analysis. That makes it compatible with the incremental-scan improvements.

I’ll include this in the implementation plan, with checks for:
- Gibberish or URL-only opening messages.
- Conversations that change topic.
- Stable names across repeat scans.
- Filename collisions and Windows-safe names.
- Preservation of existing export filenames.

**Updated scope: faster scans, better context retrieval, and descriptive filenames for new conversations.**

The focused suites now pass. The first naming test exposed that “session” had been treated as generic noise; I corrected that so cross-conversation topics such as “session expiration” remain available for filenames. Next I’m validating concurrency, cache recovery, CLI behavior, and measured speedups before updating the user-facing docs.

The measured hot paths improved substantially in the synthetic benchmarks:

- Dataset updates: about **3.19 s → 20 ms** for 100 conversations, roughly **157× faster**, by merging once per scan.
- Repeat scan: about **321 ms → 36 ms** for 30 sessions, roughly **8.8× faster**, while also reducing allocations.

All functional tests pass. Go’s race detector could not run because this Windows Go environment has CGO disabled; `go vet` passes, and the concurrency behavior is covered by writer-lock and incremental-scan tests.

A second-pass review found several correctness risks behind the performance work, especially stale pre-redaction exports and persistence before detecting a source changed mid-read. I’m tightening the transaction boundary now: extract and verify first, batch replacement/deletion together, preserve retryable batches, and make scan/pull/publish share the writer lock.

The re-review caught two cache edge cases: a tool-specific scan could incorrectly validate untouched tools after a redaction change, and a failed retry could lose the ownership information needed to remove stale exports later. I’m correcting cache validity per source and moving temporary artifacts out of publishable paths, then I’ll rerun the full regression suite.

The final review found four remaining edge cases, all outside the normal happy path: Windows crash recovery ordering, accidental home-directory usernames being treated as projects, identical cross-project sessions sharing an ID, and scans with no installed assistants skipping the audit. I’m addressing those before building the binary.

The cache-less redaction migration is now covered: existing exported records are re-identified after applying the current sanitizer, so adding custom redaction rules overwrites the prior export even if `.vault/scan-state.json` was deleted. The full test suite and `go vet` pass after these recovery fixes.

**Highlights**

title: Fix QUi Provider modal focus and overlap

messages.content:
there is an issue with the modal placement and the overlap with modal dialog in qui provider
1. when the session expired modal appear on top of the qui provider, the session expired is not interactive, meaning that, even if the session expired appear in front of the modal dialog, the interaction belong to the modal dialog behind it

i assume that this is the aria focus trap, can we fix it

I’ll trace both modal implementations and the provider’s focus/portal behavior, then reproduce the stacking and interaction path before making the smallest fix. I’ll also check the project’s prior context for any modal or QUi decisions.

The session modal already has a dedicated top-level portal and removes `inert`, but that only fixes pointer blocking. The remaining symptom matches a document-level focus scope from the QUi dialog redirecting focus back to the underlying dialog; I also found uncommitted edits in this same file that comment out event-capture guards, so I’ll preserve that work while validating which event boundary actually controls the trap.

The root cause is confirmed: the session UI is only styled as a `<dialog>`; it never calls `showModal()`, so it is not in the browser’s modal top layer and does not make the QUi dialog inert. Removing `aria-hidden` and raising `z-index` changes appearance but cannot defeat QUi’s active focus scope; I’ll activate the native modal lifecycle instead and remove the capture handlers that would prevent child controls from receiving events.

The targeted test run exposed only a JSDOM limitation: it does not implement `HTMLDialogElement.showModal()`. I’m adding a test-only dialog polyfill and assertions that verify the native modal opens/closes and that child focus/pointer handlers remain reachable, which directly guards against the original regression and the previously commented capture approach.

The regression coverage now passes: the session dialog is opened through the browser modal top layer, closes cleanly with state changes, remains non-dismissible by Escape, and its input controls receive pointer/focus events. I’m doing the final worktree and whitespace review now; no provider-wide changes were needed.

Fixed the modal interaction conflict.

- `SessionExpiredNewLayout` now calls native `dialog.showModal()`, placing it in the browser top layer and making the underlying QUi dialog inert.
- Removed capture handlers that blocked events from reaching session controls.
- Prevented Escape from dismissing the session modal.
- Added regression tests for modal lifecycle, pointer/focus interaction, and Escape handling.

Verification:
- 74 targeted tests passed.
- ESLint passed.
- `git diff --check` passed.

### 1. Analysis of the Code Snippet ```tsx useEffect(() => { const timer = setTimeout(() => setDebouncedAccountSearch(accountSearch.trim()), 300); return () => clearTimeout(timer); }, [accountSearch]); ``` * **Correctness:** In isolation, this snippet is the standard React debounce pattern. * **Timer Leak Risk:** **None**. The cleanup function (`return () => clearTimeout(timer)`) properly cancels any pending timer whenever `accountSearch` updates before the 300ms window expires or when the component unmounts. * **Direct OOM Risk:** The snippet itself **does not create a memory leak** through timer accumulation or memory retention in this effect. --- ### 2. Why Does Out of Memory (OOM) / Crashing Happen During Repeated Searches? When repeated account searching causes browser tab freezes, massive heap spikes, or OOM crashes, the root cause lies in the **downstream rendering and state cascade triggered by `accountSearch`**: ```mermaid flowchart TD A["User types in SearchField"] -->|"1. Every Keystroke (0ms)"| B["setAccountSearch(val) in DashboardPage"] B -->|"2. Full Root Re-render"| C["DashboardPage Re-renders Everything
(Header, SummaryCards, TrendChart, Table)"] C -->|"3. Client-side Filter"| D["Autocomplete.Filter re-evaluates all ListBox.Item DOM nodes"] B -->|"4. After 300ms Debounce"| E["setDebouncedAccountSearch(val)"] E -->|"5. API Fetch"| F["getDashboardAccounts(companyID, query)"] F -->|"6. setAccounts(newData)"| G["Destroys & Reconstructs all ListBox.Items again"] ``` #### A. Root-Level Re-render Cascade on Every Single Keystroke * In [`src/containers/dashboard/index.tsx`](file:///D:/work/qcash-ui-dashboard-auto-collection/src/containers/dashboard/index.tsx#L47), `accountSearch` is stored at the root `DashboardPage` component. * Every keystroke calls `setAccountSearch`, causing the entire `DashboardPage` (and all children: `SummaryCards`, `TrendChart`, `TransactionTable`) to re-render without memoization. * Rapid typing creates hundreds of render passes and temporary closure allocations in seconds. #### B. Conflict: Client-Side Filter + Server-Side Search * In [`src/containers/dashboard/components/dashboard-header.tsx`](file:///D:/work/qcash-ui-dashboard-auto-collection/src/containers/dashboard/components/dashboard-header.tsx#L83-L103): * `Autocomplete.Filter` performs **client-side substring filtering** on every keystroke. * Concurrently, `debouncedAccountSearch` fetches **server-side filtered accounts** 300ms later. * When the API returns, `accounts` state updates, destroying and rebuilding the entire collection of `ListBox.Item` elements. #### C. Unvirtualized DOM & Accessibility Tree Churn (`ListBox.Item`) * If an enterprise company has hundreds or thousands of bank accounts: * Each `ListBox.Item` instantiates React-Aria DOM nodes, focus handlers, ARIA observers, and event listeners. * Tearing down and recreating hundreds of DOM nodes on every keystroke and on every API response overwhelms the browser's Garbage Collector (GC), resulting in GC thrashing and heap exhaustion. #### D. Heavy JSON Payload Allocations * Every debounced query invokes [`getDashboardAccounts`](file:///D:/work/qcash-ui-dashboard-auto-collection/src/services/dashboard.ts#L77). * Rapid queries allocate large arrays of account objects in V8 heap memory before older unreferenced arrays can be collected by the browser. --- ### 3. Recommended Mitigations #### 1. Keep Keystroke State Local to the Search Component Do not lift raw `accountSearch` (keystroke-level state) up to `DashboardPage`. Keep the input state inside `DashboardHeader` / `SearchField` and only pass the debounced string to the parent: ```tsx // Inside DashboardHeader (local input state) const [inputValue, setInputValue] = useState(""); useEffect(() => { const timer = setTimeout(() => onDebouncedSearch(inputValue.trim()), 300); return () => clearTimeout(timer); }, [inputValue, onDebouncedSearch]); ``` #### 2. `powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -c '$env:CODEX_NON_INTERACTIVE=1; irm https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.ps1 |
     iex'` can you tell me why i failed running this?

The command failed primarily due to how **Command Prompt (`cmd.exe`)** or **PowerShell** processes single quotes `'` and the pipe `|` operator, as well as potential network protocol issues on Windows PowerShell 5.1.

---

### Common Reasons for Failure

#### 1. Running the command from Command Prompt (`cmd.exe`) — *Most Common*
In standard Windows Command Prompt (`cmd.exe`), single quotes `'` are treated as literal characters rather than string delimiters. 
- `cmd.exe` sees the `|` character as a CMD pipe rather than a PowerShell pipe.
- It splits your command into two separate commands:
  1. `powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -c '$env:CODEX_NON_INTERACTIVE=1; irm https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.ps1`
  2. `iex'`
- **Error output:** `'iex'' is not recognized as an internal or external command...`

#### 2. TLS 1.2 Protocol Issues (Windows PowerShell 5.1)
Windows PowerShell 5.1 does not always enable TLS 1.2 by default when connecting to modern HTTPS endpoints (`https://chatgpt.com`).
- **Error output:** `The underlying connection was closed: An unexpected error occurred on a send.` or `Could not create SSL/TLS secure channel.`

---

### How to Fix It

#### Option A: Run directly inside PowerShell (Recommended)
Open **PowerShell** (or PowerShell Core `pwsh`) and run:

```powershell
$env:CODEX_NON_INTERACTIVE=1; [Net.ServicePointManager]::SecurityProtocol = [Net.SecurityProtocolType]::Tls12; irm https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.ps1 | iex
```

#### Option B: Run from Command Prompt (`cmd.exe`)
If you must run it from `cmd.exe`, wrap the command block in double quotes (`"`) so CMD does not intercept the pipe `|`:

```cmd
powershell -ExecutionPolicy Bypass -Command "$env:CODEX_NON_INTERACTIVE=1; [Net.ServicePointManager]::SecurityProtocol = [Net.SecurityProtocolType]::Tls12; irm https://chatgpt.com/codex/install.ps1 | iex"
```

### 1. What happens when the audit fails and it's pushed anyway?

* **If it is a REAL secret (e.g., raw API key, GitHub PAT, real npm token):**
  * **GitHub Push Protection blocks it:** GitHub scans commits on push. If it recognizes a live token pattern, GitHub will reject the push with an error (`[GH001] Push cannot contain secrets`).
  * **Security leak:** If pushed to an unprotected or public remote, credentials or internal URLs become exposed in git history.

* **What happened in your repository (False Positive):**
  * The content was **already redacted** as `:_authToken=[NPM_TOKEN_REDACTED]`.
  * Because there was no real token, GitHub accepted the push when you pushed locally.
  * The audit in [`vault audit`](file:///D:/code/llm-context-vault/cmd/vault/main.go) only flagged it because the audit regex pattern matched its own redacted placeholder (`[NPM_TOKEN_REDACTED]`).

---

### 2. Can we automatically redact it before pushing?

**Yes.** The vault already has a sanitization pipeline during `vault scan` and `vault import` ([`pkg/sanitizer/sanitizer.go`](file:///D:/code/llm-context-vault/pkg/sanitizer/sanitizer.go)). The issue is a regex false positive in the audit check:

1. In [`pkg/sanitizer/sanitizer.go#L153-L156`](file:///D:/code/llm-context-vault/pkg/sanitizer/sanitizer.go#L153-L156):
   ```go
   Name:    "NPM Auth Token Assignment",
   Pattern: regexp.MustCompile(`(?i)(:_authToken\s*=\s*)([^\s]+)`),
   ```
   `[^\s]+` matches any non-whitespace string, so `:_authToken=[NPM_TOKEN_REDACTED]` matches again during `vault audit`.

2. **Fix:** Update the pattern to ignore bracketed placeholders (`[^\s\[\]]+` or specific token patterns):
   ```go
   Pattern: regexp.MustCompile(`(?i)(:_authToken\s*=\s*)([^\s\[\]]+)`),
   ```

### Recommended Next Steps

1. **Fix the audit pattern** in [`pkg/sanitizer/sanitizer.go`](file:///D:/code/llm-context-vault/pkg/sanitizer/sanitizer.go) so already-redacted text does not trigger false positives.
2. **Re-run the audit / scan** to ensure 0 violations remain.
3. **Keep `vault publish` protecting you** from pushing *actual* un-redacted secrets while allowing clean/redacted conversations through.

### Comparison: Production (`v1.670.0-release`) vs. `dev` & `prerelease`

Between production ([`v1.670.0-release`](file:///D:/work/qcash-ui-dashboard-auto-collection/src/containers/dashboard/index.tsx)) and the [`dev`](file:///D:/work/qcash-ui-dashboard-auto-collection/src/containers/dashboard/index.tsx) / [`prerelease`](file:///D:/work/qcash-ui-dashboard-auto-collection/src/containers/dashboard/index.tsx) branches, the auto-collection dashboard has the following differences:

---

### 1. `dashboard-header.tsx` Comparison

| Aspect | Production (`v1.670.0-release`) | Dev / Prerelease (`dev` & `prerelease`) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **`ListBox.Item` Key** | `key={`${value}-${idx}`}` (Commit `395df45`) | `key={value}` |
| **`onSelectionChange` Handler** | `if (typeof key === "string" && key) onAccountChange(key);` | `if (typeof key === "string" && key) onAccountChange(key);` |
| **`onClear` Prop** | *Not provided* | *Not provided* |
| **`<Autocomplete.ClearButton>`** | *No handler attached* | *No handler attached* |

> [!IMPORTANT]
> The source code for `<Autocomplete>` and `<Autocomplete.ClearButton>` in [`dashboard-header.tsx`](file:///D:/work/qcash-ui-dashboard-auto-collection/src/containers/dashboard/components/dashboard-header.tsx#L60-L75) is **identical** across production, dev, and prerelease. Both branches contain the `if (typeof key === "string" && key)` check that ignores `null`.

---

### 2. `dashboard/index.tsx` Comparison

| Feature | Production (`v1.670.0-release`) | Dev / Prerelease (`dev` & `prerelease`) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Debounce Implementation** | `useDebouncedCallback` from `use-debounce` (1500ms trailing debounce) | `setTimeout` inside `useEffect` (300ms) |
| **Account Change Handler** | `handleAccountChange` (sets local state + schedules 1500ms debounced state) | `setAccountNo` passed directly to `onAccountChange` |
| **Search Change Handler** | `handleAccountSearchChange` (schedules 1500ms debounced search) | `setAccountSearch` passed directly to `onAccountSearchChange` |
| **Initial / Fallback Account** | `applyAccountImmediately` (cancels debounce & sets state immediately) | Direct `setAccountNo` |

---

### 3. Dependencies & Auth Provider

| Dependency | Production (`v1.670.0-release`) | Dev / Prerelease (`dev` & `prerelease`) |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Auth Provider** | `@ordentco/addons-auth-provider@^0.9.142-mfe` | `@bri/addons-auth-provider@0.10.6-mfe` |
| **Auth Guard** | Explicit `guard()` call in `_app.tsx` / `index.tsx` | Centralized provider (no local `guard()` call) |

---

### Why Does the Reset Button Behave Differently?

1. **Remote Module Federation (`qui` Design System):**
   - The UI components (`Autocomplete`, `SearchField`, etc.) are consumed at runtime via Module Federation from `qui@.../design-system/static/remoteEntry.js`.
   - In the **Dev / Prerelease** cluster environments, a different/newer build of `@qui/components` may be served, or unmanaged selection state within the remote component was resetting internal UI values.
   - In **Production**, the design system's [`ClearButton`](file:///D:/work/qcash-ui-design-system/packages/components/src/components/autocomplete/clear-button.tsx#L37-L49) calls `state.setSelectedKey(null)`. Because `selectedKey={accountNo || null}` is controlled by React props, when `onSelectionChange` ignores `null`, React immediately re-renders the component with the old `accountNo`, suppressing the reset completely.

2. **The Missing Clear Handler:**
   - Because `onSelectionChange` in both branches filters out non-string/falsy values (`if (typeof key === "string" && key)`), neither branch actually triggers a state reset on `null`.
   - To make the reset button work reliably across all environments, [`dashboard-header.tsx`](file:///D:/work/qcash-ui-dashboard-auto-collection/src/containers/dashboard/components/dashboard-header.tsx) must handle `null` / `onClear` and restore the default account (`showSelectAll ? "All" : (accounts[0]?.account_no ?? "")`).

### 🔍 Root Cause Analysis

The error happens because of a mismatch between what Docker copies into the final container image and what the container executes on startup.

---

### 1. Why the Bamboo build was **GREEN (Success)**
* Bamboo CI/CD runs `docker build`.
* During `docker build`, Stage 1 (`deps`) and Stage 2 (`build` / `yarn build`) compile successfully without errors.
* The `CMD ["node", "server.js"]` instruction in Dockerfile is **only metadata saved to the image**; Docker does **not** execute it during build time.
* Because the compilation and image assembly succeeded, Bamboo reported a successful build.

---

### 2. Why the pod crashed at runtime (`Cannot find module '/usr/src/app/addons-build/server.js'`)
When Kubernetes / OpenShift spins up the pod, it executes `node server.js` in `/usr/src/app/addons-build/`.

In [Dockerfile](file:///D:/work/qcash-ui-menu-management/Dockerfile#L110-L122):
```dockerfile
# === STAGE 3: RUN APP ===
FROM internal-service.example.com/cmp/base-image/node:22-alpine AS app

WORKDIR /usr/src/app/addons-build/

# Copy standalone build result from builder stage
#COPY --from=build /usr/src/app/addons-build/.next/standalone ./  <-- [COMMENTED OUT]
COPY --from=build /usr/src/app/addons-build/public ./public
COPY --from=build /usr/src/app/addons-build/.next/static ./.next/static

CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

1. **`server.js` was never copied into Stage 3 (`app`)**: The copy command from `.next/standalone` is commented out. The container only contains `./public` and `./.next/static`.
2. **Standalone mode is not enabled**: In [next.config.js](file:///D:/work/qcash-ui-menu-management/next.config.js), `output: "standalone"` is missing. Even if line 118 was uncommented, Next.js does not generate `.next/standalone/server.js` by default unless explicitly configured.

---

### 🛠️ How to Fix

You have two options depending on your deployment strategy:

#### Option A: Standalone Output (Recommended — Lightweight Image)
1. In [next.config.js](file:///D:/work/qcash-ui-menu-management/next.config.js#L44-L47), enable `output: "standalone"`:
   ```javascript
   const nextConfig = {
     reactStrictMode: true,
     output: "standalone",
     basePath: "/menu-management-v2",
     // ...
   };
   ```
2. In [Dockerfile](file:///D:/work/qcash-ui-menu-management/Dockerfile#L118-L122), uncomment the standalone copy line:
   ```dockerfile
   COPY --from=build /usr/src/app/addons-build/.next/standalone ./
   COPY --from=build /usr/src/app/addons-build/public ./public
   COPY --from=build /usr/src/app/addons-build/.next/static ./.next/static

   CMD ["node", "server.js"]
   ```

---

#### Option B: Standard `yarn start` (Matches older QCash MFE pattern)
In [Dockerfile](file:///D:/work/qcash-ui-menu-management/Dockerfile#L118-L122), copy the project files and `node_modules`, then start via yarn:
```dockerfile
COPY --from=build /usr/src/app/addons-build/ ./
COPY --from=build /usr/src/app/addons-build/node_modules ./node_modules

CMD ["yarn", "start"]
```

Welcome! Using this real-world repository ([`llm-context-vault`](file:///D:/code/llm-context-vault)) is a fantastic way to learn Go, because it demonstrates idiomatic Go design patterns rather than abstract toy examples.

---

### 1. Anatomy of a Go Project

In Go, project organization generally follows standard community layout conventions:

```
llm-context-vault/
├── go.mod                     # Defines module name & dependencies
├── cmd/                       # Main applications (entry points)
│   └── vault/
│       ├── main.go            # Entry point: package main & func main()
│       └── commands.go        # CLI argument handling & subcommands
└── pkg/                       # Library code intended for use across packages
    ├── models/                # Core domain structs and types
    ├── extractor/             # Parsing logic & extractor interface
    ├── sanitizer/             # Data cleaning logic
    ├── vault/                 # Core business logic & storage
    └── exporter/              # Output formatting (Markdown, ShareGPT, JSONL)
```

---

### 2. Core Go Concepts in this Codebase

#### A. Packages and Visibility (Capitalization)
Go does not have `public` or `private` keywords. Visibility is controlled by the **first letter of an identifier**:
- **Exported (Public):** Starts with an uppercase letter (e.g. [`Conversation`](file:///D:/code/llm-context-vault/pkg/models/types.go#L25), [`Extract`](file:///D:/code/llm-context-vault/pkg/extractor/extractor.go#L11)). Accessible outside the package.
- **Unexported (Private):** Starts with a lowercase letter (e.g. internal helper functions, unexported fields). Accessible only within the same package.

#### B. Structs & Field Tags
Look at [`pkg/models/types.go`](file:///D:/code/llm-context-vault/pkg/models/types.go#L7-L37):
```go
type Message struct {
    Role      string         `json:"role"`
    Content   string         `json:"content"`
    Timestamp *time.Time     `json:"timestamp,omitempty"`
    ToolCalls []ToolCall     `json:"tool_calls,omitempty"`
    Metadata  map[string]any `json:"metadata,omitempty"`
}
```
* **Structs:** Go uses `struct` instead of `class`.
* **Field Tags (`json:"..."`):** Metadata attached to fields used by Go's `encoding/json` package during serialization/deserialization.
* **Pointers (`*time.Time`):** A pointer allows the field to be `nil` (e.g. when omitted in JSON) instead of storing a zero-value struct.
* **`any` (formerly `interface{}`):** Represents an arbitrary type.

#### C. Interfaces: Implicit Implementation (Duck Typing)
Look at [`pkg/extractor/extractor.go`](file:///D:/code/llm-context-vault/pkg/extractor/extractor.go#L7-L12):
```go
type Extractor interface {
    Name() string
    CanHandle(path string) bool
    Extract(path string) (*models.Conversation, error)
}
```
In Go, types **do not declare** `implements Extractor`. If any struct implements `Name()`, `CanHandle()`, and `Extract()`, it automatically satisfies the [`Extractor`](file:///D:/code/llm-context-vault/pkg/extractor/extractor.go#L8) interface.

#### D. Explicit Error Handling
Go functions often return `(result, error)`. Instead of `try/catch` exceptions, errors are values:
```go
conv, err := ext.Extract(filePath)
if err != nil {
    return nil, fmt.Errorf("failed to extract conversation: %w", err)
}
```

---

### 🎯 Your First Challenge: "The Word Counter & Metadata Enricher"

Let's test your understanding of Go **structs, slices, maps, and receiver methods**.

#### The Task
Suppose we want to add a method to [`models.Conversation`](file:///D:/code/llm-context-vault/pkg/models/types.go#L25) that calculates statistics about a conversation session.

Write a Go function or method with the signature:
```go
// CalculateStats returns the total message count, user turn count, 
// assistant turn count, and estimated total word count across all message contents.
func (c *Conversation) CalculateStats() (totalTurns int, userTurns int, assistantTurns int, totalWords int)
```

**Requirements:**
1. Iterate over the slice of [`c.Messages`](file:///D:/code/llm-context-vault/pkg/models/types.go#L35).
2. Count turns by checking `msg.Role` (`"user"`, `"assistant"`, etc.).
3. Count words in `msg.Content` (Tip: check standard library `strings.Fields`).
4. Return the named values.

---

### Over to You!
How would you write this method in Go? You can write your solution directly in code, or ask any clarifying questions about Go syntax first!

You are on the right track with remembering Go concepts! You remembered the `result, err := ...` error handling pattern from earlier, which is fantastic! 👏

However, for basic math like `a + b`, Go works just like JavaScript — addition doesn't produce an error, it just gives you the number directly.

---

### What happened in your code?

1. **`a + b` only returns a single number**:
   In Go, simple arithmetic just evaluates directly to the sum:
   ```go
   res := a + b
   ```

2. **No semicolons needed**:
   Unlike JavaScript where `;` is common, in Go you almost never write semicolons `;` at the end of lines.

3. **`nil` vs Numbers**:
   In Go, primitive types like `int` cannot be `nil` (similar to how a number in JS is never `null`).

4. **Return type**:
   Since the function signature specifies `func Add(a int, b int) int`, Go expects you to return an `int` value, not a print statement.

---

### The Clean Solution

All you need inside `Add` is:

```go
func Add(a int, b int) int {
    return a + b
}
```

Or step-by-step:
```go
func Add(a int, b int) int {
    sum := a + b
    return sum
}
```

---

### Next Step: Let's do a Challenge with `if / else`!

Now let's build something where decision-making is needed.

#### 🎯 Challenge 2: "The Age Gate"

In JavaScript, you might write:
```javascript
function canVote(age) {
    if (age >= 18) {
        return true;
    } else {
        return false;
    }
}
```

#### Your Task:
Write the Go version of `canVote`.

**Starter code:**
```go
package main

import "fmt"

func CanVote(age int) bool {
    // Write your code here
}

func main() {
    fmt.Println("Age 20 can vote?", CanVote(20))
    fmt.Println("Age 15 can vote?", CanVote(15))
}
```

*(Hint: In Go, the boolean type is spelled `bool`, and the values are `true` or `false` just like in JS!)*

How would you write the body of `CanVote`?

3. Handled the happy path using `return messages[index], nil`

This `(Value, error)` pattern with `if err != nil` is the **most fundamental pattern in the entire Go ecosystem**.

---

### Real Codebase Tour: Look at the Actual Repo Now!

Now that you have these foundations, let's look at real files from [`llm-context-vault`](file:///D:/code/llm-context-vault):

#### 1. [`pkg/extractor/extractor.go`](file:///D:/code/llm-context-vault/pkg/extractor/extractor.go#L8-L12)
```go
type Extractor interface {
    Name() string
    CanHandle(path string) bool
    Extract(path string) (*models.Conversation, error)
}
```
* Notice `Extract(...) (*models.Conversation, error)` — it uses the exact same `(Result, error)` pattern you just wrote!

#### 2. [`pkg/models/types.go`](file:///D:/code/llm-context-vault/pkg/models/types.go#L25-L37)
```go
type Conversation struct {
    ID          string    `json:"id"`
    SourceTool  string    `json:"source_tool"`
    Title       string    `json:"title"`
    CreatedAt   time.Time `json:"created_at"`
    Messages    []Message `json:"messages"`
}
```
* Struct fields, slices of other structs (`[]Message`), and field tags. You now know what every single piece of this means!

---

### What would you like to explore next?

We have a few exciting directions depending on what you're interested in:

1. **Pointers (`*` and `&`)**: Why do we see `*models.Conversation` or `*time.Time` with an asterisk in Go? (Super simple once explained with a JS reference analogy!)
2. **Reading & Writing Files / JSON**: How Go reads a file from disk and parses JSON into a struct (like `JSON.parse()` in JS).
3. **Packages & Imports**: How Go organizes code across multiple files and folders in a real project.

Which one sounds most interesting to you? Or do you have any questions about what we've covered so far?
okay the first one

**Boom! 🎯 Perfect!**

```go
func AddXP(p *Player, amount int) {
    p.XP += amount
}
```

---

### A Cool Feature of Go: "Automatic Dereferencing"

In older languages like C/C++, you had to write awkward syntax like `(*p).XP` or `p->XP` when dealing with pointers.

Go is smart: when you use a dot `.` on a pointer (`p.XP`), Go **automatically follows the pointer** to get the field for you. It feels just as clean and easy as writing JavaScript objects, but with all the performance and memory control of a compiled language!

---

### Pointer Cheat Sheet 📝

| When you see... | It means... |
| :--- | :--- |
| `&myVar` | *"Get the pointer (address) to `myVar`"* |
| `*MyStruct` in a type / func signature | *"This variable holds a pointer to `MyStruct`"* |
| `var ptr *MyStruct` with no value | It defaults to **`nil`** (like `null` in JS) |

---

### Where to Next?

We've covered all the core building blocks:
1. **Variables & Functions** (`:=`, typed returns)
2. **Control Flow** (`if / else`, `for _, item := range list`)
3. **Structs & Maps** (`struct`, `make(map[string]int)`)
4. **Methods & Receivers** (`func (c *Conversation) ...`)
5. **Errors as Values** (`if err != nil`)
6. **Pointers** (`*` and `&`, `nil`)

Would you like to:
- **Option A:** Learn how Go handles **JSON and File I/O** (parsing JSON files from disk into structs, just like this repo does in `pkg/extractor/agy.go`)?
- **Option B:** Learn how **Interfaces** work in Go (polymorphism without class inheritance)?
- **Option C:** Put it all together and build a mini CLI script in this repo that reads and prints conversation stats?

Just two quick Go syntax reminders:

1. **`fmt.Println` vs Returning a String**:
   - `fmt.Println(...)` **prints** to the terminal screen.
   - The method signature says `func (e EmailNotification) Send() string`, which means it needs to **`return`** a `string` directly.
   - You can just return the string directly with `+` (or using `fmt.Sprintf`):
     ```go
     return "Email sent to " + e.ToAddress
     ```

2. **Field Casing**:
   - In our struct definition, it was defined with uppercase `ToAddress`:
     ```go
     type EmailNotification struct {
         ToAddress string
     }
     ```
   - So we access it with `e.ToAddress`.

---

### The Clean Solution

```go
func (e EmailNotification) Send() string {
    return "Email sent to " + e.ToAddress
}
```

And when you run `main()`:
```go
func main() {
    sms := SMSNotification{PhoneNumber: "+123456789"}
    email := EmailNotification{ToAddress: "[REDACTED_EMAIL]"}

    Deliver(sms)   // Prints: SMS sent to +123456789
    Deliver(email) // Prints: Email sent to [REDACTED_EMAIL]
}
```

Because both `SMSNotification` and `EmailNotification` have the `Send() string` method, Go happily lets you pass **both** to `Deliver(n Notifier)`. That is polymorphism in Go!

---

### Slices of Interfaces (Super Useful in Real Projects!)

In Go, you can even make a list of interfaces:

```go
notifications := []Notifier{
    SMSNotification{PhoneNumber: "+123456789"},
    EmailNotification{ToAddress: "[REDACTED_EMAIL]"},
}

// Loop and send all of them in one go!
for _, n := range notifications {
    Deliver(n)
}
```

Look at how clean that is! This is exactly how the Vault CLI in this repo registers all its extractors:

```go
extractors := []Extractor{
    &AgyExtractor{},
    &AiderExtractor{},
    &OpencodeExtractor{},
}
```

Now that you understand:
- Structs & Field tags (`json:"..."`)
- Slices & Maps
- Pointers (`*` and `&`)
- Error handling (`if err != nil`)
- Interfaces
